title: Reliable transferable forecasting of volcanic eruptions

concept.text: The innovation would be a dependable way to forecast the likelihood of a volcanic eruption within a stated time window, with useful warning time and uncertainty that matches observed outcomes, across different volcanic systems. Transferability means retaining forecasting skill at volcanoes whose eruption histories were not used to develop the method, including systems with limited local records. Successful forecasts already exist; the proposed advance is to make useful forecasting more broadly transferable and prospectively reliable.

The central task is to distinguish unrest that will culminate in eruption from unrest that will subside. Seismic activity can provide evidence, but the proposed capability would need to work within the constraints of available observations and expert interpretation. Forecasting whether an eruption is likely is distinct from forecasting its magnitude, geographic effects or consequences. The supplied study advances seismic transfer learning; it does not establish this broader operational capability.

significance.text: If achieved, reliable transfer would reduce dependence on having many previously recorded eruptions at each individual volcano. That would extend a capability demonstrated at selected well-observed systems toward volcanoes with scarce local training histories and limited observatory resources. The revolutionary change would be broader access to useful warning information despite the rarity and diversity of eruptions, rather than the first successful eruption forecast.

As a conditional impact assessment, better forecasts could support decisions about warnings, intensified observation and deployment of monitoring resources. Calibrated uncertainty would help decision-makers interpret both elevated risk and continued uncertainty during unrest. These are plausible applications of the proposed capability, not operational benefits measured by the supplied study.

Benefits would depend on observations, local hazard assessment and effective response. A forecast of eruption likelihood would not by itself establish eruption size, identify affected areas or guarantee reduced losses. Likewise, transfer to a volcano with a short eruption record should not be equated with forecasting at a volcano with no instrumentation. Some eruptions have subtle or no known precursors, potentially leaving too little observable warning time for the intended decisions.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a forecasting method whose skill survives changes in volcanic system, eruption behavior and monitoring conditions, and remains dependable when deployed on future data. A model must identify genuinely transferable precursors while distinguishing them from local patterns and non-eruptive unrest. Scarce eruption histories make that distinction difficult: a method can appear successful on a limited collection of past events without having demonstrated reliable future performance.

Concrete barriers include differences in physical precursors, short or incomplete monitoring records, station placement and distance, and eruption styles outside the training experience. The supplied study discusses a missed eruption in relation to a short record, station distance or potentially different precursors; those explanations remain alternatives rather than an established diagnosis. Its exclusion of effusive episodes also leaves a substantive boundary on the demonstrated scope.

Another gap is converting useful discrimination into trustworthy probabilities and operational warnings. The study's scores are explicitly non-probabilistic: ranking periods by apparent eruption risk does not establish that a stated probability corresponds to the observed frequency of eruptions. Real-time processing must also avoid using information unavailable when a forecast would have been issued. Long non-eruptive periods are essential to determining whether apparent sensitivity comes at an impractical false-alarm cost.

A potential physical limit is insufficient observable lead time. Reports of subtle or absent known precursors support retaining this possibility, but they do not prove that every such eruption is fundamentally unforeseeable. Better observations or different measurements might reveal information that existing monitoring missed; whether they would provide useful warning remains unresolved.

current_state.text: Successful eruption forecasts predate the proposed innovation. The supplied article discusses historical examples including Pinatubo and Redoubt. These demonstrate that useful forecasting is possible in some circumstances, while leaving open the harder question of dependable transfer across volcanoes with different histories, precursors and observation networks.

Published in Nature Communications on February 25, 2025, “Ergodic seismic precursors and transfer learning for short term eruption forecasting at data scarce volcanoes” used seismic data from 41 eruptions at 24 volcanoes over 73 years. Its leave-one-volcano-out evaluation tested transfer to volcanoes excluded from training. The supplied review reports that the method achieved higher pooled discrimination than the study's seismic-amplitude benchmark, RSAM. This comparison supports progress within the evaluated dataset; it does not establish superiority over complete observatory practice.

The evaluated episodes were selected abrupt eruptive events; effusive episodes were excluded. The model did not estimate eruption magnitude, and its output scores were not probabilities. Consequently, the results do not demonstrate calibrated eruption likelihoods, coverage of all eruption styles or performance at uninstrumented volcanoes. The paper presents a possible complement to observatory monitoring and expert interpretation, with operational readiness still premature.

The evaluation was retrospective or pseudo-prospective rather than a true prospective deployment. Full-record normalization introduced a potential information-leakage limitation acknowledged by the authors. They performed a limited sensitivity check, but that check did not turn the experiment into a test using only information available in real time. Withholding entire volcanoes is meaningful evidence of transfer, yet it does not guarantee that the same performance would occur on future observations.

The supplied research initially relied on the author-hosted abstract because publisher and PMC access failed or encountered a challenge. The subsequent supplied review reports access to a retained, internally identified 12-page article and bases its findings on explicit article text and extracted table values. Supplementary materials and figure images were not inspected. The hosting page's AI-generated explainers were not treated as independent corroboration. These limits constrain the available assessment without invalidating the documented results.

The supplied evidence establishes a dated 2025 advance. It contains no freshness search establishing whether later work changed the field by November 1, 2026. The present record therefore cannot determine whether subsequent studies have resolved any of the prospective, calibration or coverage limitations.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: register the forecasting method, forecast windows, evaluation rules and intended deployment scope before testing, then issue time-stamped probabilistic forecasts on future observations. Keep the model frozen during each declared evaluation period, or specify update rules in advance. Independent evaluators should assess performance at diverse volcanoes excluded from development, including substantial periods of non-eruptive unrest and ordinary background activity. These are proposed safeguards, not an established completion standard.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered prospective forecasts undergo independent evaluation at held-out volcanoes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed performance assessment: compare forecasts with both simple baselines and relevant local practice using the information available at forecast time. Report calibration, missed eruptions, false alarms, warning duration and the distribution of lead times. Define useful lead time, acceptable performance and evaluation duration before testing, in relation to the decisions the forecasts are intended to support. No universal numerical threshold for these quantities is established by the supplied evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Forecast performance against baselines and local practice is reported

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility assessment: make the data, preprocessing, model versions and forecast records available to independent investigators as far as access permits. Reproduce the analysis with normalization and all other processing restricted to information available when each forecast was issued. An independent implementation and prospective replication would provide stronger evidence than repeating the same retrospective experiment.
completion_criteria.label: Independent investigators reproduce analyses using only forecast-time information

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scope assessment: report results separately by eruption style, monitoring conditions and amount of local history. State where the method cannot issue a useful forecast and whether limited observations require abstention or greater uncertainty. Include difficult cases with short or absent known precursors, without presuming that every eruption must be forecastable. Finite tests could establish demonstrated breadth across the evaluated conditions, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Forecasting limits are reported across evaluated volcanic conditions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: demonstrate that the forecasts can be interpreted alongside observatory observations and hazard assessments for specified warning decisions. Keep claims about eruption magnitude, affected areas and loss reduction separate unless those capabilities receive their own validation. A convincing demonstration of eruption-likelihood forecasting would not automatically demonstrate them.
completion_criteria.label: Forecasts are interpretable alongside observatory assessments for specified warning decisions

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: GEO-01, “Reliable short-term forecasting of damaging earthquakes,” has the closest methodological overlap. Both concern forecasting rare geophysical events, distinguishing precursors from background activity, and evaluating uncertainty, missed events and false alarms. Their physical targets and available precursors differ, so success in volcanic eruption forecasting would not establish earthquake forecasting capability.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-02, “A chemically and thermally resolved map of Earth’s deep interior,” and GEO-08, “Establishing when and how sustained plate tectonics began,” concern aspects of Earth's internal structure and evolution that provide broad context for volcanism. GEO-10 instead targets near-term behavior at individual volcanic systems. Deep-Earth mapping or a reconstruction of tectonic origins would not by itself supply operational eruption forecasts.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-03, “Geothermal reservoirs engineered economically in ordinary deep rock,” GEO-04, “Global-scale, verifiable mineral storage of carbon dioxide,” and GEO-06, “Discovery of globally consequential recoverable geological hydrogen,” share interests in subsurface characterization, fluids or geological monitoring. Their central goals are energy production, carbon storage and resource discovery, respectively. Any shared measurement or modeling methods would be enabling overlaps rather than completion of GEO-10 or those separate innovations.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-09, “Predictive laws linking erosion, sediment transport and landscape evolution,” shares the ambition of finding predictive relationships that transfer across geological settings. Its principal targets are surface processes and landscape change, whereas GEO-10 concerns eruption onset and warning time. Forecasting an eruption would also remain separate from predicting subsequent sediment transport or landscape effects.

Roster-based synthesis: GEO-05, “Recovery of a detailed geological record of Earth’s first half-billion years,” and GEO-07, “Reconstructing the Moon-forming impact from independent geological evidence,” primarily seek reconstructions of ancient events from surviving evidence. They share challenges of incomplete observations and competing explanations, but their retrospective objectives differ from GEO-10's prospective forecasting requirement. All remain distinct entries.

unresolved_issues: Whether work after the February 2025 study changed the field by November 1, 2026 is unresolved because the supplied record contains no freshness search.
Useful lead times, acceptable false-alarm and missed-eruption performance, calibration targets and evaluation duration remain to be specified for particular warning decisions.
Prospective transfer performance across eruption styles, monitoring conditions and volcanoes with scarce local histories remains unestablished by the supplied evidence.
The operational effect of full-record normalization is not fully resolved by the reported limited sensitivity check.
The relative roles of short records, station distance and different precursors in the discussed missed eruption remain uncertain.
The extent to which better observations could provide useful lead time for eruptions with subtle or absent known precursors remains unresolved.
Supplementary materials and figure images were not inspected in the supplied review; conclusions are limited to the article text and extracted table values described there.

brief.title: Dependable eruption warnings across different volcanoes
possible: People living near a restless volcano could get a dependable estimate of whether it will erupt within a stated period, with enough warning to inform decisions. Those estimates would remain useful at volcanoes whose past eruptions were not used to develop the method, including places with little local history.
why: Observatories with scarce eruption records could gain access to useful forecasting. Warning decisions would depend less on having recorded many eruptions at the same volcano.
Trustworthy estimates of uncertainty could help officials decide when to issue warnings, intensify observation or move monitoring resources as volcanic activity changes.

sources.who: Alberto Ardid, David Dempsey and collaborators
sources.showed: A model learned warning patterns in ground vibrations across volcanoes. In tests on volcanoes excluded from its training, it distinguished approaching eruptions from other activity better than a simple vibration-strength benchmark.
sources.quote:
our
approach forecasts eruptions at unobserved (out-of-sample) volcanoes.
sources.cited_for: Patterns learned at other volcanoes can help forecast eruptions where local training records are scarce.
sources.not_established: The tests did not establish dependable future forecasts or probabilities that match how often eruptions actually occur.

sources.showed: Their model classified volcanic activity from ground-vibration patterns across different volcanoes, including eruptions that explode and those that release flowing lava. They reported warning periods ranging from hours to days.
sources.quote: classifies the state of volcanic hazard in near real-time and estimates a probability of the occurrence of an eruption, resulting in a period from at least hours to several days to forecast an eruption.
sources.cited_for: Tests across different volcanic systems support the possibility of shared warning patterns.
sources.not_established: The results do not establish independently evaluated forecasts on future observations or dependable probabilities across volcanoes.

shown: Ardid and colleagues tested their approach across 24 volcanoes, withholding each volcano from training in turn. This demonstrated transfer in past observations. The tests excluded eruptions involving flowing lava, and the model's scores were not probabilities.

Successful eruption forecasts already exist at selected volcanoes. Dependable forecasts across different systems remain unproven: the transfer tests used past observations, and some data processing used information that would not have been available when a warning was needed.
missing: Independently evaluated forecasts on future observations at volcanoes excluded from development, including long periods without eruptions.
Trustworthy eruption probabilities with useful warning times and an acceptable balance of missed eruptions and false alarms.
Independent reproduction using only information available when each forecast would have been issued.
Demonstrated usefulness across eruption styles, monitoring conditions and short local histories, alongside observatory assessments.

milestones.label: Independent tests of future forecasts at unfamiliar volcanoes
milestones.explanation: Independent evaluators would assess time-stamped probabilities at volcanoes excluded from development, under rules fixed before testing. This would test whether forecasting skill survives future activity, including periods without eruptions.

milestones.label: Forecast performance compared with simpler methods and local practice
milestones.explanation: Comparisons would report probability accuracy, missed eruptions, false alarms and warning times against simpler methods and local practice. Standards set before testing would tie success to intended warning decisions.

milestones.label: Independent reproduction without information from the future
milestones.explanation: Independent investigators would reproduce the analysis using only information available when each forecast was issued. A separate implementation and replication on future observations would strengthen confidence in the result.

milestones.label: Forecasting limits established across volcanic conditions
milestones.explanation: Results would distinguish eruption styles, monitoring conditions and local histories, including cases requiring greater uncertainty or no forecast. This would establish where useful forecasting has been demonstrated.

milestones.label: Forecasts usable alongside observatory assessments
milestones.explanation: Forecasts would have to be interpretable alongside observatory observations and hazard assessments for specified warning decisions. This would establish practical usefulness without implying predictions of eruption size or affected areas.

uncertain: How much warning is useful, and what balance of false alarms and missed eruptions is acceptable, depends on the decision.
It remains unclear how much using information from the full observation period inflated the reported forecasting performance.
Some eruptions have subtle or no known warning signs; whether better observations could provide useful warning remains unresolved.

page.title: Transferable probabilistic eruption forecasting
page.definition: A fixed method estimates the probability that an instrumented volcano will erupt within 48 hours and outperforms a constant eruption-rate forecast on future observations at volcanoes excluded from development. The capability covers magmatic eruptions, which emit new magma, and phreatic eruptions, driven by steam.

goal.need: Local forecasting models need recorded eruptions from which to learn; the seismic archive below illustrates their scarcity. At Whakaari, the eruption on 9 December 2019 killed 22 tourists and guides and severely injured 26 others. Quantified eruption likelihood informs volcano-access decisions and disaster response.

completion.title: Transferred eruption probabilities beat a fixed eruption-rate forecast on future observations.
completion.criterion: A frozen model issues 48-hour eruption probabilities at instrumented volcanoes whose eruptions were excluded from development, using only information available at issue time. On future eruptive and non-eruptive observations, its mean logarithmic score, mean[y ln(p)+(1−y) ln(1−p)], exceeds that of a local eruption-rate probability fixed before testing; p is the issued probability and y is 1 for eruption within 48 hours and 0 otherwise. The advantage must hold at the declared target volcanoes in both tracked cases. This minimum establishes probability skill; operational warning-time and calibration tolerances remain unspecified.
completion.set_by: Atlas minimum combining published forecast-verification tests; no external completion criterion was found.
completion.basis: Searches of National Academies and USGS forecasting goals, IAVCEI and WMO guidance, prize criteria and validation papers found no external completion threshold for cross-volcano eruption probabilities. This minimum combines “evaluation of a frozen model on future data” with logarithmic skill above the published zero reference. It establishes prospective transfer of probability skill; operational acceptance requirements remain unspecified.

milestones.title: Local eruption probabilities achieve logarithmic skill above 0 on a withheld eruption.
milestones.criterion: For an eruption excluded from forecast-model and probability-calibration training, a local forecast attains scaled logarithmic skill >0 against a constant eruption-rate probability. At Whakaari, a phreatic volcano, Dempsey and colleagues reported 0.33 over 2 December 2019 to 18 December 2019; six earlier eruptions supplied training and the eruption on 9 December 2019 was withheld. This is retrospective evidence.
milestones.set_by: Community forecast-verification convention, implemented by Dempsey and colleagues in equations (5)–(6). Their published application concerns Whakaari’s phreatic eruptions.
milestones.threshold_quote: a reference of 0 for models that perform as well as one uninformed by data

milestones.title: Transferred forecasts discriminate pre-eruptive periods at withheld volcanoes with AUC above 0.5.
milestones.criterion: Without training on the target volcano’s eruptions, a model distinguishes the 48 hours before eruption from non-eruptive intervals with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) >0.5. Ardid and colleagues reported AUC 0.81 for the magmatic pool (9 volcanoes, 16 eruptions) and 0.80 for the phreatic pool (6 volcanoes, 15 eruptions). Their tests used full-record normalization, excluded effusive episodes and produced scores rather than probabilities. Rey-Devesa and colleagues evaluated six eruptive datasets from five volcanoes, including effusive activity; this does not establish the same whole-volcano AUC test.
milestones.set_by: Community discrimination reference of AUC=0.5, explicitly applied to leave-one-volcano-out forecasting by Ardid and colleagues. This is a discrimination test, without an operational acceptance threshold.
milestones.threshold_quote: a reference AUC of 0.5, which denotes no discrimination of eruptions.

milestones.title: A frozen transferred model discriminates future pre-eruptive periods with AUC above 0.5.
milestones.criterion: A model frozen before deployment, with target-volcano eruptions excluded from training, achieves AUC >0.5 on future eruptive and non-eruptive observations using a 48-hour eruption window. Inputs and preprocessing use only information available at issue time. This tests prospective discrimination before probability skill. The local Whakaari deployment from February 2020 to August 2021 recorded three false positives and no eruptions. The follow-up published on 26 August 2026 evaluated transferred forecasts at five volcanoes using past observations.
milestones.set_by: Atlas minimum combining the published frozen-model prospective test and AUC=0.5 reference. Searches found no externally specified acceptance criterion combining prospective testing with cross-volcano transfer.

not_found: No prospective evaluation establishing transferred discrimination or probability skill on both eruptive and non-eruptive future observations was located for either tracked mechanism.
No magmatic result matching the local 48-hour logarithmic-skill test was located in the checked studies.

results.finding: At Mt. Etna, one magmatic dataset, the model identified the pre-eruptive state at least 10–15 hours before eruption.
results.detail: The retrospective evaluation reports lead time, not 48-hour AUC. It left one dataset out at a time; two datasets came from Bezymianny, so leaving out a dataset did not always exclude the target volcano from training.
results.quote: Upon observing our case studies, we notice that the model determines the beginning of the pre-eruptive state between at least 10–15 h before the beginning of the eruption in the worst case, which is the lava fountains at Mt. Etna, and several days in the best case, like Volcán de Colima or Mount St. Helens;

results.finding: At Mount St. Helens, one phreatic dataset, the model identified the pre-eruptive state several days before eruption.
results.detail: The retrospective evaluation left the target dataset out of training but reports lead time rather than AUC for the 48 hours before eruption.
results.quote: Upon observing our case studies, we notice that the model determines the beginning of the pre-eruptive state between at least 10–15 h before the beginning of the eruption in the worst case, which is the lava fountains at Mt. Etna, and several days in the best case, like Volcán de Colima or Mount St. Helens;

results.finding: At Whakaari, one withheld phreatic eruption had a 48-hour forecast probability up to 400 times the background.
results.detail: The forecast was evaluated retrospectively under pseudo-prospective conditions, with the December 2019 eruption withheld from training. The supplied text does not report its scaled logarithmic skill against the constant eruption-rate forecast.
results.quote: When applied pseudo-prospectively in the 48 h prior to the December 2019 eruption, it indicated an eruption probability up to 400 times higher than the background.

results.finding: Transferred forecasts for 9 magmatic volcanoes and 16 eruptions achieved AUC 0.81.
results.detail: Whole-volcano cross-validation used a 48-hour eruption window. Full-record normalization could leak future information; effusive episodes were excluded, and outputs were scores rather than probabilities.

results.finding: Transferred forecasts for 6 phreatic volcanoes and 15 eruptions achieved AUC 0.80.
results.detail: Whole-volcano cross-validation used a 48-hour eruption window. Full-record normalization could leak future information; outputs were scores rather than probabilities.

results.finding: Retrospective transferred forecasts for 9 magmatic volcanoes and 16 eruptions achieved AUC 0.81.
results.detail: The evaluation was pseudo-prospective, not a frozen model tested on future observations. Full-record normalization also incorporated future data.

results.finding: Retrospective transferred forecasts for 6 phreatic volcanoes and 15 eruptions achieved AUC 0.80.
results.detail: The evaluation was pseudo-prospective, not a frozen model tested on future observations. Full-record normalization also incorporated future data.

results.finding: At Whakaari, prospective testing recorded 3 false positives and no eruptions.
results.detail: The model was trained on Whakaari eruptions, so it was not transferred to a withheld volcano. With no eruptions during testing, prospective discrimination and AUC could not be assessed.
results.quote: There were no eruptions in this period, and therefore, the discussion is limited to the three false positives that occurred.
